claim: The 'building-block' model of inositol trisphosphate (IP3)-mediated Ca2+ liberation posits that cell-wide cytosolic Ca2+ signals arise through coordinated activation of localized Ca2+ puffs generated by stationary clusters of IP3 receptors (IP3Rs).
source: The 'building-block' model of inositol trisphosphate (IP3)-mediated Ca2+ liberation posits that cell-wide cytosolic Ca2+ signals arise through coordinated activation of localized Ca2+ puffs generated by stationary clusters of IP3 receptors (IP3Rs).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this model.

claim: The rising phase of global Ca2+ signals is punctuated by a flurry of puffs, which terminate before the peak by a mechanism involving partial ER Ca2+ depletion.
source: We find the rising phase of global Ca2+ signals is punctuated by a flurry of puffs, which terminate before the peak by a mechanism involving partial ER Ca2+ depletion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing puff activity during global Ca2+ signals and its termination.

claim: A second mode of spatiotemporally diffuse Ca2+ signaling exists that continues after puffs terminate.
source: The continuing rise in Ca2+, and persistence of global signals even when puffs are absent, reveal a second mode of spatiotemporally diffuse Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations showing continued Ca2+ elevation after puff cessation.

claim: Puffs make only small, transient contributions to global Ca2+ signals, which are sustained by diffuse release of Ca2+ through a functionally distinct process.
source: Puffs make only small, transient contributions to global Ca2+ signals, which are sustained by diffuse release of Ca2+ through a functionally distinct process.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Ca2+ release contributions shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ signals generated by the liberation of Ca2+ ions sequestered in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through inositol trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) channels regulate ubiquitous cellular processes as diverse as gene transcription, secretion, mitochondrial energetics, electrical excitability and fertilization.
source: Cytosolic Ca2+ signals generated by the liberation of Ca2+ ions sequestered in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) through inositol trisphosphate receptor (IP3R) channels regulate ubiquitous cellular processes as diverse as gene transcription, secretion, mitochondrial energetics, electrical excitability and fertilization (Clapham, 2007; Berridge et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Cells achieve unique repertories of Ca2+-dependent functions by generating a hierarchy of cytosolic Ca2+ signals with markedly different spatial scales and temporal durations, ranging from brief, localized Ca2+ transients called puffs to larger and more prolonged Ca2+ elevations that engulf the cell.
source: Cells achieve such unique repertories of Ca2+-dependent functions by generating a hierarchy of cytosolic Ca2+ signals with markedly different spatial scales and temporal durations, ranging from brief, localized Ca2+ transients called puffs (Parker and Yao, 1991; Yao et al., 1995) to larger and more prolonged Ca2+ elevations that engulf the cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Global elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ typically last several seconds and may appear as waves that propagate throughout the cell.
source: Global elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ typically last several seconds and may appear as waves that propagate throughout the cell (Woods et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Global Ca2+ elevations can recur as oscillations with periods between a few seconds and a few minutes, and are thought to encode information in a 'digital' manner, whereby increasing stimulus strength results predominantly in an increase in frequency rather than amplitude.
source: They can recur as oscillations with periods between a few seconds and a few minutes, and are thought to encode information in a 'digital' manner, whereby increasing stimulus strength results predominantly in an increase in frequency rather than amplitude (Parekh, 2011; Smedler and Uhlén, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Puffs are tightly localized elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ generated by stationary clusters containing small numbers of IP3Rs, which last only tens or a few hundreds of milliseconds and remain restricted within a few micrometers.
source: Puffs, on the other hand, are tightly localized elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ generated by stationary clusters containing small numbers of IP3Rs, which last only tens or a few hundreds of milliseconds and remain restricted within a few micrometers (Bootman et al., 1997a; Parker et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The opening of IP3R channels is regulated by cytosolic Ca2+ itself, in addition to IP3.
source: Crucially, the opening of IP3R channels is regulated by cytosolic Ca2+ itself, in addition to IP3.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge of IP3R function.

claim: Low concentrations of Ca2+ increase the open probability of the IP3R channel whereas high concentrations favor a closed state.
source: Low concentrations of Ca2+ increase the open probability of the channel whereas high concentrations favor a closed state (Parker and Ivorra, 1990; Iino, 1990; Bezprozvanny et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Biphasic modulation of IP3Rs by Ca2+ leads to the phenomenon of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR).
source: This biphasic modulation of IP3Rs by Ca2+ leads to the phenomenon of Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release (CICR).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of IP3R function.

claim: Ca2+ diffusing from one open IP3R channel may trigger the opening of adjacent channels, with self-reinforcing CICR countered by Ca2+ feedback inhibition.
source: Ca2+ diffusing from one open channel may thus trigger the opening of adjacent channels, with self-reinforcing CICR countered by Ca2+ feedback inhibition.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of CICR mechanism.

claim: CICR may remain locally restricted to a single cluster, containing from a few to a few tens of functional IP3Rs, to produce a puff.
source: CICR may remain locally restricted to a single cluster, containing from a few to a few tens of functional IP3Rs, to produce a puff; whereas it is proposed that a global response is generated by successive cycles of CICR and Ca2+ diffusion acting over longer spatial ranges to recruit successive puff sites (Bootman et al., 1997a; Parker et al., 1996; Berridge, 1997; Bootman and Berridge, 1996; Callamaras et al., 1998; Dawson et al., 1999; Marchant, 2001; Marchant et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A global Ca2+ response is proposed to be generated by successive cycles of CICR and Ca2+ diffusion acting over longer spatial ranges to recruit successive puff sites.
source: CICR may remain locally restricted to a single cluster, containing from a few to a few tens of functional IP3Rs, to produce a puff; whereas it is proposed that a global response is generated by successive cycles of CICR and Ca2+ diffusion acting over longer spatial ranges to recruit successive puff sites (Bootman et al., 1997a; Parker et al., 1996; Berridge, 1997; Bootman and Berridge, 1996; Callamaras et al., 1998; Dawson et al., 1999; Marchant, 2001; Marchant et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research proposing this model.

claim: Recent theoretical simulations have questioned whether Ca2+ released through puff activity is alone sufficient to propagate global cytosolic Ca2+ signals.
source: However, the transition between these modes remains an area of active investigation (Rückl and Rüdiger, 2016; Miyamoto and Mikoshiba, 2019; Sneyd et al., 2017a; Sneyd et al., 2017b; Rückl et al., 2015), and recent theoretical simulations have questioned whether Ca2+ released through puff activity is alone sufficient to propagate global cytosolic Ca2+ signals (Piegari et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent theoretical work.

claim: Ca2+ puffs are often evident during the initial rising phase of global Ca2+ signals.
source: Although Ca2+ puffs are often evident during the initial rising phase of global Ca2+ signals (Bootman et al., 1997a; Bootman and Berridge, 1996; Marchant, 2001; Marchant et al., 1999), a challenge in answering this question arises because puffs become obscured as the overall cytosolic Ca2+ level continues to increase.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior observations.

claim: Puffs become obscured as the overall cytosolic Ca2+ level continues to increase during global Ca2+ signals.
source: Although Ca2+ puffs are often evident during the initial rising phase of global Ca2+ signals (Bootman et al., 1997a; Bootman and Berridge, 1996; Marchant, 2001; Marchant et al., 1999), a challenge in answering this question arises because puffs become obscured as the overall cytosolic Ca2+ level continues to increase.
evidence: This claim is based on established observational challenges in the field.

claim: Fluctuation analysis can reveal and monitor temporally rapid and spatially confined Ca2+ transients (puffs) during even large amplitude global Ca2+ elevations.
source: To reveal and monitor temporally rapid and spatially confined Ca2+ transients (puffs) during even large amplitude global Ca2+ elevations we developed image processing and analysis routines to analyze local fluctuations in Ca2+ fluorescence signals (Ellefsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by the development and application of the method described in the manuscript.

claim: Rapid flurries of Ca2+ puffs accompany the rising phase of global Ca2+ signals evoked by photoreleased IP3 and by agonist stimulation of the IP3 signaling pathway.
source: We find that rapid flurries of Ca2+ puffs accompany the rising phase of global Ca2+ signals evoked by photoreleased IP3 and by agonist stimulation of the IP3 signaling pathway, but these rapidly terminate before the peak of the response through a mechanism regulated by ER Ca2+ store content.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ca2+ puffs rapidly terminate before the peak of the global Ca2+ response through a mechanism regulated by ER Ca2+ store content.
source: We find that rapid flurries of Ca2+ puffs accompany the rising phase of global Ca2+ signals evoked by photoreleased IP3 and by agonist stimulation of the IP3 signaling pathway, but these rapidly terminate before the peak of the response through a mechanism regulated by ER Ca2+ store content.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The punctate liberation of Ca2+ via transient, localized Ca2+ puffs contributes only a small fraction of the total Ca2+ liberated during global Ca2+ signals.
source: The punctate liberation of Ca2+ via transient, localized Ca2+ puffs contributes only a small fraction of the total Ca2+ liberated during global Ca2+ signals, which are instead sustained by diffuse Ca2+ liberation through a functionally distinct mode of release.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Global Ca2+ signals are sustained by diffuse Ca2+ liberation through a functionally distinct mode of release.
source: The punctate liberation of Ca2+ via transient, localized Ca2+ puffs contributes only a small fraction of the total Ca2+ liberated during global Ca2+ signals, which are instead sustained by diffuse Ca2+ liberation through a functionally distinct mode of release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing continued Ca2+ elevation after puff cessation.

claim: The two modes of IP3-mediated Ca2+ liberation have important implications for downstream signaling, imparting spatial and kinetic specificity to Ca2+-dependent effector functions and Ca2+ transport.
source: These two modes of IP3-mediated Ca2+ liberation have important implications for downstream signaling, imparting spatial and kinetic specificity to Ca2+-dependent effector functions and Ca2+ transport.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings about two modes of Ca2+ release.

claim: The fluctuation analysis algorithm applies a spatial filter (Gaussian blur with sigma ~1 µm) and a band-pass temporal Butterworth filter (3–20 Hz) to the raw fluorescence image stack.
source: Beginning with a black level-subtracted 'raw' fluorescence image stack, our algorithm applied a spatial filter (Gaussian blur with sigma ~1 µm), and a band-pass temporal Butterworth filter (3–20 Hz).
evidence: This describes the technical method used in the study.

claim: The fluctuation analysis algorithm calculates the standard deviation (SD) of the fluorescence signal at each pixel throughout a 160 ms running boxcar window.
source: The resulting image stack was then processed by a running boxcar window (160 ms) that, for each pixel, calculated the standard deviation (SD) of the fluorescence signal at that pixel throughout the duration of the window.
evidence: This describes the technical method used in the study.

claim: The fluctuation analysis algorithm corrects for photon shot noise by subtracting a scaled measure of the square root of fluorescence intensity at each pixel.
source: Lastly, the algorithm corrected for photon shot noise by subtracting a scaled measure of the square root of fluorescence intensity at each pixel.
evidence: This describes the technical method used in the study.

claim: Photoreleased i-IP3 evoked a widespread increase in fluorescence throughout the cell that peaked within about 5 s.
source: Photoreleased i-IP3 evoked a widespread increase in fluorescence throughout the cell that peaked within about 5 s, during which time several transient, local 'hot spots' were evident.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Several transient, local 'hot spots' were evident during the rising phase of the global Ca2+ signal evoked by photoreleased i-IP3.
source: Photoreleased i-IP3 evoked a widespread increase in fluorescence throughout the cell that peaked within about 5 s, during which time several transient, local 'hot spots' were evident.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The power spectrum obtained during the rise of the global Ca2+ signal showed much greater power at frequencies between about 1–20 Hz as compared to the control spectrum.
source: Strikingly, the spectrum obtained during the rise of the global Ca2+ signal showed much greater power at frequencies between about 1–20 Hz as compared to the control spectrum, rolling off at higher frequencies to a noise floor determined by photon shot noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In HEK 3KO cells (devoid of IP3Rs), ionomycin evoked a slow liberation of Ca2+ from intracellular stores without any evident hot spots of local transients in the SD images.
source: Figure 1F shows snapshots of 'raw' fluorescence captured before (i) and during (ii-v) application of ionomycin. The fluorescence rose uniformly throughout the cell without any evident hot spots of local transients in the SD images (Figure 1G and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F-J.

claim: Mean spectra from HEK 3KO cells treated with ionomycin displayed flat, substantially uniform distributions of power across all frequencies, consistent with photon shot noise increasing in proportion to the mean fluorescence level.
source: Mean spectra from these regions (Figure 1I) displayed flat, substantially uniform distributions of power across all frequencies, consistent with photon shot noise increasing in proportion to the mean fluorescence level.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: SD signals from local ROIs and from a ROI encompassing the entire HEK 3KO cell showed no increase in fluctuations beyond that expected for photon shot noise during ionomycin-evoked Ca2+ elevation.
source: Notably, SD signals from local ROIs (Figure 1J, superimposed black traces) and from a ROI encompassing the entire cell (yellow trace) showed no increase in fluctuations beyond that expected for photon shot noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Temporal SD signals faithfully reflect transient, localized Ca2+ puff activity while minimizing confounding contributions from shot noise and slower changes in global fluorescence.
source: We thus conclude that the temporal SD signals faithfully reflect transient, localized Ca2+ puff activity while minimizing confounding contributions from shot noise and slower changes in global fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of temporal and spatial SD analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Under basal conditions, the shot noise-corrected cell-wide SD signals were almost flat, with a mean around zero, indicating a negligible level of local Ca2+ activity at rest.
source: Under basal conditions, the shot noise-corrected cell-wide SD signals were almost flat, with a mean around zero (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1), indicating a negligible level of local Ca2+ activity at rest.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Photorelease of small amounts of i-IP3 by brief (~100 ms) UV flashes evoked Ca2+ puffs without generating any appreciable global rise in basal Ca2+.
source: Photorelease of small amounts of i-IP3 by brief (~100 ms) UV flashes evoked Ca2+ puffs - directly visible in the Cal520 fluorescence ratio movie in Figure 2—video 1, and more evident as sharp transients in the whole-cell SD trace - but without generating any appreciable global rise in basal Ca2+ (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Longer UV flashes (200–1000 ms) generated whole-cell elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ that rose and fell over several seconds, with fluorescence signals reaching peak amplitudes in rough proportion to the flash duration.
source: Longer flashes (200–1000 ms) generated whole-cell elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ that rose and fell over several seconds, with fluorescence signals reaching peak amplitudes in rough proportion to the flash duration (smooth traces, Figure 2C–E; Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: SD movies and whole-cell SD traces revealed an underlying flurry of localized, transient Ca2+ events during the rising phase of the global Ca2+ responses evoked by longer UV flashes.
source: SD movies (Figure 2—video 2) and whole-cell SD traces (noisy traces, Figure 2C–E) revealed an underlying flurry of localized, transient Ca2+ events during the rising phase of the global Ca2+ responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-E and associated videos.

claim: In instances where global Ca2+ signals were small and slowly rising, the SD traces showed Ca2+ transients persisting throughout the prolonged rising phase.
source: In instances where global Ca2+ signals were small and slowly rising, the SD traces showed Ca2+ transients persisting throughout the prolonged rising phase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For cells exhibiting intermediate and fast rising global signals, SD traces revealed Ca2+ fluctuations that began almost immediately following photorelease of i-IP3, reached a maximum during the rising phase of the global signal, but then declined almost to baseline by the peak of the response.
source: On the other hand, the SD traces from cells exhibiting intermediate (Figure 2D) and fast rising (Figure 2E) global signals revealed Ca2+ fluctuations that began almost immediately following photorelease of i-IP3, reached a maximum during the rising phase of the global signal, but then declined almost to baseline by the peak of the response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Overall Ca2+ levels continued to rise after puffs had largely ceased, and cytosolic Ca2+ remained elevated for several seconds during which time Ca2+ fluctuations were largely suppressed.
source: Notably, overall Ca2+ levels continued to rise after puffs had largely ceased, and cytosolic Ca2+ remained elevated for several seconds in the face of rapid removal from the cytosol, during which time Ca2+ fluctuations were largely suppressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In all three categories where global Ca2+ signals were evoked, the mean SD signals were transient, indicating that puff activity was largely confined to the rising phase of the global Ca2+ elevation and largely ceased by the time the global signal reached a maximum.
source: Notably, in all three categories where global Ca2+ signals were evoked (Figure 2C–E) the mean SD signals were transient, indicating that puff activity was largely confined to the rising phase of the global Ca2+ elevation and largely ceased by the time the global signal reached a maximum.
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The durations of the puff flurries progressively shortened with increasing rates of rise in global Ca2+.
source: The durations of the puff flurries progressively shortened with increasing rates of rise in global Ca2+ and the magnitudes of the SD signal at the peak of the flurry activity increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The magnitudes of the SD signal at the peak of the flurry activity increased with increasing rates of rise in global Ca2+.
source: The durations of the puff flurries progressively shortened with increasing rates of rise in global Ca2+ and the magnitudes of the SD signal at the peak of the flurry activity increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by pooled data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A brief (5 s) pulse of carbachol (CCH) elicited a rapid, global rise in Ca2+ that was accompanied by an underlying burst of local Ca2+ signals.
source: A brief (5 s) pulse of CCH elicited a rapid, global rise in Ca2+ that was accompanied by an underlying burst of local Ca2+ signals (Figure 2F; Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fluctuations arising from local Ca2+ signals during CCH-evoked responses occurred predominantly during the initial portion of the rising phase and then subsided to near basal levels before the peak of the global response.
source: As with responses evoked by photoreleased i-IP3, fluctuations arising from local Ca2+ signals occurred predominantly during the initial portion of the rising phase and then subsided to near basal levels before the peak of the global response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Peak fluorescence amplitudes were similar for CCH-evoked and i-IP3-evoked responses (ΔF/F0 of 8.89 ± 0.3 for CCH vs. 7.27 ± 0.4 for i-IP3).
source: Peak fluorescence amplitudes were similar to mean values for 11 cells stimulated by strong photorelease of i-IP3 (ΔF/F0 of 8.89 ± 0.3 for CCH vs. 7.27 ± 0.4 for i-IP3);
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of data from CCH and i-IP3 stimulation.

claim: The rising phase kinetics of the global Ca2+ signal were similar for CCH-evoked and i-IP3-evoked responses (rise from 20% to 80% of peak 0.70 s ± 0.05 s for CCH vs. 0.80 s ± 0.06 s for i-IP3).
source: as were the rising phase kinetics of the global Ca2+ signal (rise from 20% to 80% of peak 0.70 s ± 0.05 s for CCH vs. 0.80 s ± 0.06 s for i-IP3).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of data from CCH and i-IP3 stimulation.

claim: Global Ca2+ elevations evoked by CCH decayed more rapidly than those evoked by i-IP3 (fall from 80% to 20% of peak 6.33 s ± 0.3 s for CCH vs 20.05 s ± 3.2 s for i-IP3).
source: However, global Ca2+ elevations evoked by CCH decayed more rapidly than those evoked by i-IP3 (fall from 80% to 20% of peak 6.33 s ± 0.3 s for CCH vs 20.05 s ± 3.2 s for i-IP3) - likely because the slowly-degraded i-IP3 evoked a more sustained release of Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of data from CCH and i-IP3 stimulation.

claim: The slowly-degraded i-IP3 likely evoked a more sustained release of Ca2+ compared to CCH.
source: However, global Ca2+ elevations evoked by CCH decayed more rapidly than those evoked by i-IP3 (fall from 80% to 20% of peak 6.33 s ± 0.3 s for CCH vs 20.05 s ± 3.2 s for i-IP3) - likely because the slowly-degraded i-IP3 evoked a more sustained release of Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of i-IP3 and the observed decay kinetics.

claim: Although the amplitudes of the SD signals were greater for the faster rising responses, all cells showed similar 'inverted U' shaped relationships between SD signal and Ca2+ level.
source: Although the amplitudes of the SD signals were greater for the faster rising responses, all cells showed similar 'inverted U' shaped relationships.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In all three groups of cells (fast, intermediate, and slow rising responses), the SD signal was maximal when the Cal520 fluorescence ratio reached a ΔF/F0 value of about two and then declined progressively as global Ca2+ rose higher.
source: In all three groups, the SD signal was maximal when the Cal520 fluorescence ratio reached a ΔF/F0 value of about two and then declined progressively as global Ca2+ rose higher.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: A closely similar inverted U relationship between SD signal and Ca2+ level was observed for Ca2+ elevations evoked by CCH.
source: A closely similar inverted U relationship was observed for Ca2+ elevations evoked by CCH (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The decline in SD signal at higher Ca2+ levels during global signals cannot be attributed to a failure of the algorithm to detect local fluctuations because of saturation of the Cal520 indicator dye.
source: The decline in SD signal at higher Ca2+ levels during global signals cannot be attributed to a failure of our algorithm to detect local fluctuations because of saturation of the Cal520 indicator dye.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence presented in the text and figures.

claim: Maximal fluorescence responses evoked by addition of ionomycin in high (10 mM) Ca2+-containing medium (ΔF/F0 of 18.93 ± 1.5; n = 32 cells) considerably exceeded the peak fluorescence level evoked by even strong photorelease of i-IP3 (mean ΔF/F0 7.27 ± 0.4, n = 11 cells).
source: Notably, maximal fluorescence responses evoked by addition of ionomycin in high (10 mM) Ca2+-containing medium (ΔF/F0 of 18.93 ± 1.5; n = 32 cells) considerably exceeded the peak fluorescence level evoked by even strong photorelease of i-IP3 (mean ΔF/F07.27 ± 0.4, n = 11 cells), and were greatly in excess of the fluorescence level (ΔF/F0 ~2; Figure 3) at which the SD signal began to decline.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing ionomycin and i-IP3 responses.

claim: Instances of local Ca2+ signals were observed even during large global Ca2+ elevations (ΔF/F0 >8).
source: Moreover, we observed instances of local Ca2+ signals even during large global Ca2+ elevations (ΔF/F0 >8; Figure 3—figure supplement 1),
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SD signals using the lower affinity indicator fluo8L (Kd 1.86 µM vs. 320 nM for Cal520) confirmed that puff activity was similarly suppressed prior to the peak of i-IP3 evoked Ca2+ elevations.
source: and obtained SD signals using the lower affinity indicator fluo8L (Kd 1.86 µM vs. 320 nM for Cal520) confirming that puff activity was similarly suppressed prior to the peak of i-IP3 evoked Ca (Berridge et al., 2000) elevations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cell-wide Ca2+ responses and flurries of local Ca2+ signals in cells bathed in solutions containing 2 mM Ca2+ closely matched the patterns of activity in cells imaged in the absence of extracellular Ca2+.
source: Cell-wide Ca2+ responses and flurries of local Ca2+ signals closely matched the patterns of activity in cells imaged in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–G),
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Scatter plots of SD signal vs. global Ca2+ fluorescence signal in the presence of 2 mM extracellular Ca2+ mirrored those in the absence of extracellular Ca2+.
source: and scatter plots of SD signal vs. global Ca2+ fluorescence signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 3H,I) mirrored those in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3H,I.

claim: The puff activity during IP3-evoked global Ca2+ elevations appears independent of Ca2+ influx into the cell.
source: Thus, the puff activity during IP3-evoked global Ca2+ elevations appears independent of Ca2+ influx into the cell.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of responses in the presence and absence of extracellular Ca2+.

claim: Global Ca2+ responses decayed more slowly when Ca2+ was included in the bath solution (fall80-20 for strong photoreleased i-IP3 of 35.87 s ± 3.9 s in 2 mM Ca2+ vs. 20.05 s ± 3.2 s in zero Ca2+; Fall80-20 for CCH of 13.06 s ± 0.5 s in 2 mM Ca2+ vs 6.33 s ± 0.3 in zero Ca2+).
source: However, global Ca2+ responses decayed more slowly when Ca2+ was included in the bath solution (fall80-20 for strong photoreleased i-IP3 of 35.87 s ± 3.9 s in 2 mM Ca2+ vs. 20.05 s ± 3.2 s in zero Ca2+; Fall80-20 for CCH of 13.06 s ± 0.5 s in 2 mM Ca2+ vs 6.33 s ± 0.3 in zero Ca2+).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of decay kinetics.

claim: Influx through slowly activating store-operated channels likely prolongs the response when extracellular Ca2+ is present.
source: A likely explanation is that influx through slowly activating store-operated channels prolongs the response when extracellular Ca2+ is present.
evidence: This is an inference based on known mechanisms of store-operated Ca2+ entry.

claim: Mean traces of whole-cell Ca2+ fluorescence (ΔF/F0) and associated SD fluctuations in FCCP-treated cells stimulated with CCH exhibited local and global Ca2+ signals similar to vehicle-treated controls, although with slightly smaller peak magnitudes.
source: Mean traces of whole-cell Ca2+ fluorescence (ΔF/F0) and associated SD fluctuations in FCCP-treated cells stimulated with CCH exhibited local and global Ca2+ signals similar to vehicle-treated controls, although with slightly smaller peak magnitudes (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Scatter plots of SD signal vs. bulk Ca2+ level during the rising phase of CCH-evoked Ca2+ elevations were closely similar in control and following FCCP application.
source: Scatter plots of SD signal vs. bulk Ca2+ level during the rising phase of CCH-evoked Ca2+ elevations were closely similar in control and following FCCP application (Figure 3—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4E.

claim: Although the SD signals evoked by CCH declined progressively with increasing prior photorelease of Ca2+, this reduction was matched by a similar diminution in peak amplitudes (ΔF/F0) of the global Ca2+ signal.
source: Although the SD signals evoked by CCH declined progressively with increasing prior photorelease of Ca2+, this reduction was matched by a similar diminution in peak amplitudes (ΔF/F0) of the global Ca2+ signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mean ratios of puff activity (integral under SD traces) relative to the size of the CCH-evoked global Ca2+ signal remained almost constant for all Ca2+ jumps evoked by photolysis of caged Ca2+, even at levels (ΔF/F0 >6) corresponding to those where puff activity was strongly suppressed during the rising phase of global responses.
source: Mean ratios (Figure 4B, filled symbols) remained almost constant for all Ca2+ jumps; even at levels (ΔF/F0 >6) corresponding to those where puff activity was strongly suppressed during the rising phase of global responses (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The cell showed a typical flurry of puff activity like that in non-EGTA-loaded cells when loaded with EGTA by incubation with 15 μM EGTA-AM.
source: The cell showed a typical flurry of puff activity like that in non-EGTA-loaded cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Puffs ceased before the peak of the global Ca2+ signal in EGTA-loaded cells, even though the amplitude of the signal (2.5 ΔF/F0) was strongly attenuated.
source: Puffs ceased before the peak of the global Ca2+ signal, even though the amplitude of the signal (2.5 ΔF/F0) was strongly attenuated.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In EGTA-loaded cells, the peak SD signal was attained at a fluorescence level of about 0.40 ΔF/F0 vs. about 2 ΔF/F0 for controls.
source: Notably, the peak SD signal was attained at a fluorescence level of about 0.40 ΔF/F0 vs. about 2 ΔF/F0 for controls, and puffs were substantially suppressed at fluorescence levels (ΔF/F0 ~2) where the puff activity was near maximal in control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Puffs were substantially suppressed at fluorescence levels (ΔF/F0 ~2) in EGTA-loaded cells where the puff activity was near maximal in control cells.
source: Notably, the peak SD signal was attained at a fluorescence level of about 0.40 ΔF/F0 vs. about 2 ΔF/F0 for controls, and puffs were substantially suppressed at fluorescence levels (ΔF/F0 ~2) where the puff activity was near maximal in control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of IP3Rs by elevated cytosolic [Ca2+] is not the primary mechanism causing puff activity to terminate during whole-cell Ca2+ responses.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that inhibition of IP3Rs by elevated cytosolic [Ca2+] is not the primary mechanism causing puff activity to terminate during whole-cell Ca2+ responses.
evidence: This claim is based on the results from experiments with prior Ca2+ elevation and EGTA buffering.

claim: The decline in SD signal during the rising phase of the response does not arise because the indicator dye becomes saturated, but faithfully reflects a physiological termination of puff activity.
source: They further buttress other evidence that the decline in SD signal during the rising phase of the response does not arise because the indicator dye becomes saturated, but faithfully reflects a physiological termination of puff activity.
evidence: This claim is based on multiple lines of evidence excluding indicator saturation as a cause.

claim: Following wash-out of CPA and maintenance in Ca2+-free medium for about 4 min, the resting cytosolic Ca2+ level had returned close to the original baseline, and photorelease of i-IP3 evoked a substantial elevation in global Ca2+, yet the SD signal showed almost no transient puff activity during this response.
source: Following wash-out of CPA, the cell was maintained in Ca2+-free medium so that the cellular Ca2+ content (including that of the ER) gradually depleted owing to passive and active extrusion across the plasma membrane. After about 4 min the resting cytosolic Ca2+ level had returned close to the original baseline, and we delivered a photolysis flash to photorelease i-IP3. This evoked a substantial elevation in global Ca2+, yet the SD signal showed almost no transient puff activity during this response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells in both groups (Ca2+-containing and Ca2+-free medium after CPA treatment) showed substantial global Ca2+ responses that were not appreciably different in peak amplitudes.
source: Cells in both groups showed substantial global Ca2+ responses that were not appreciably different in peak amplitudes (Figure 5E);
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Puff activity was strongly suppressed in cells maintained in zero Ca2+ medium after CPA treatment, whereas cells in Ca2+-containing medium showed robust puff activity during the rising phase of the response.
source: but whereas the SD signals showed that puff activity was strongly suppressed in cells maintained in zero Ca2+ medium, cells in Ca2+-containing medium showed robust puff activity during the rising phase of the response (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In both cases (repeated CCH application in Ca2+-containing and Ca2+-free solutions), the amplitudes of the global Ca2+ signals progressively declined, likely a result of inhibition of IP3Rs.
source: In both cases, the amplitudes of the global Ca2+ signals progressively declined, likely a result of inhibition of IP3Rs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decline in response amplitude.

claim: Whereas the amplitude of puff activity reported by SD signals in cells bathed in Ca2+-containing medium fell roughly in proportion to the amplitude of the global fluorescence signal, puff activity in Ca2+-free medium declined abruptly.
source: However, whereas the amplitude of puff activity reported by SD signals in cells bathed in Ca2+-containing medium fell roughly in proportion to the amplitude of the global fluorescence signal, puff activity in Ca2+-free medium declined abruptly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: For cells in Ca2+-containing medium, the mean ratio of puff activity vs. peak global Ca2+ amplitude remained constant across successive CCH stimuli.
source: For cells in Ca2+-containing medium, the mean ratio remained constant across successive stimuli (blue squares, Figure 5I), whereas it declined almost to zero for cells in Ca2+-free medium (red circles, Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: For cells in Ca2+-free medium, the mean ratio of puff activity vs. peak global Ca2+ amplitude declined almost to zero across successive CCH stimuli.
source: For cells in Ca2+-containing medium, the mean ratio remained constant across successive stimuli (blue squares, Figure 5I), whereas it declined almost to zero for cells in Ca2+-free medium (red circles, Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Ca2+ puff activity is modulated by ER Ca2+ store content.
source: We conclude from these results that Ca2+ puff activity is modulated by ER Ca2+ store content, and that when stores are partially depleted IP3 can still evoke Ca2+ release by a process that is independent of puff activity, and occurs without detectable temporal fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is based on the results from ER depletion experiments.

claim: When stores are partially depleted, IP3 can still evoke Ca2+ release by a process that is independent of puff activity, and occurs without detectable temporal fluctuations.
source: We conclude from these results that Ca2+ puff activity is modulated by ER Ca2+ store content, and that when stores are partially depleted IP3 can still evoke Ca2+ release by a process that is independent of puff activity, and occurs without detectable temporal fluctuations.
evidence: This claim is based on the results from ER depletion experiments.

claim: All three major IP3R isoforms – types 1, 2, and 3 – are expressed in WT HEK and HeLa cells.
source: In common with many other cell types, WT HEK and HeLa cells express all three major IP3R isoforms – types 1, 2, and 3 – that are encoded by separate genes and translated into structurally and functionally distinct proteins that co-translationally oligomerize to form heterotetrameric channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about these cell lines.

claim: All three IP3R isoforms can individually mediate Ca2+ puffs.
source: We (Lock et al., 2018) and others (Mataragka and Taylor, 2018) recently demonstrated that all three isoforms can individually mediate Ca2+ puffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: All three single-isoform-expressing cell lines exhibited patterns of responses qualitatively similar to WT cells, showing flurries of puffs during the foot and rising phase of global Ca2+ signals that ceased before the time of the peak global Ca2+ elevation.
source: All three single-isoform-expressing cell lines exhibited patterns of responses qualitatively similar to WT cells. The SD traces showed flurries of puffs during the foot and rising phase of global Ca2+ signals that ceased before the time of the peak global Ca2+ elevation (Figure 6A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cells expressing IP3R1 generated whole-cell Ca2+ signals having much smaller amplitudes and slower rising phases than WT and R2- and R3-expressing cells, and localized fluctuations persisted longer.
source: Cells expressing IP3R1 generated whole-cell Ca2+ signals having much smaller amplitudes and slower rising phases than WT and R2- and R3-expressing cells, and localized fluctuations persisted longer (Figure 6C,D,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C,D,I.

claim: IP3R2-expressing cells displayed fast rising, large amplitude Ca2+ signals, with a transient flurry of Ca2+ fluctuations concentrated during the initial portion of the rising phase.
source: In contrast, IP3R2-expressing cells displayed fast rising, large amplitude Ca2+ signals, with a transient flurry of Ca2+ fluctuations concentrated during the initial portion of the rising phase (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Ca2+ signals in cells expressing IP3R3 were similar in amplitude to WT and IP3R2-expressing cells, but with slower rates of rise and more prolonged flurries of puffs.
source: Ca2+ signals in cells expressing IP3R3 (Figure 6G,H) were similar in amplitude to WT and IP3R2-expressing cells, but with slower rates of rise and more prolonged flurries of puffs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: Ca2+ fluctuations were maximal when Cal520 fluorescence (ΔF/F0) rose to roughly 1.5, 6, and 3 for types 1, 2, and 3 IP3Rs, respectively.
source: Ca2+ fluctuations were maximal when Cal520 fluorescence (ΔF/F0) rose to roughly 1.5, 6, and 3 for types 1, 2, and 3 IP3Rs, respectively; and similarly large differences were evident in the global Ca2+ level attained when puff activity terminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: Stimulation of HeLa cells with histamine evoked global Ca2+ signals accompanied by flurries of local Ca2+ activity during the rising phase, which subsided as Ca2+ levels continued to rise.
source: Stimulation of HeLa cells with histamine also evoked global Ca2+ signals accompanied by flurries of local Ca2+ activity during the rising phase, which subsided as Ca2+ levels continued to rise (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SD images revealed local Ca2+ transients that began soon after photorelease of i-IP3, and before any appreciable rise in the global Ca2+ signal.
source: Similar to observations with TIRF imaging, the SD images revealed local Ca2+ transients that began soon after photorelease, and before any appreciable rise in the global Ca2+ signal (Figure 7A, panel ii).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Discrete Ca2+ events continued during much of the rising phase of the global signal but had largely ceased at the time of the peak global signal in lattice light-sheet imaging.
source: Discrete events then continued during much of the rising phase of the global signal (panels iii-v) but had largely ceased at the time of the peak global signal (panel vi).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In both cells imaged by lattice light-sheet microscopy, the local Ca2+ activity monitored by SD fluctuations started within a few hundred ms of the photolysis flash and was maximal during the early portion of the rising phase.
source: In both cells, the local Ca2+ activity monitored by SD fluctuations started within a few hundred ms of the photolysis flash and was maximal during the early portion of the rising phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The SD signal then declined, returning close to baseline as the global Ca2+ signal approached a peak in lattice light-sheet imaging.
source: The SD signal then declined, returning close to baseline as the global Ca2+ signal approached a peak.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: On average, mean SD signals from the cell interior were about one quarter of that at the periphery.
source: On average, however, mean SD signals from the cell interior were about one quarter of that at the periphery, and fluctuations arising from interior sites followed a similar relation with bulk Ca2+ level as peripheral sites (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The diffuse component of the Ca2+ rise observed by TIRF microscopy cannot be accounted for by Ca2+ spreading from punctate release at internal sites and becoming blurred by diffusion in space and time.
source: Given the relatively low average level of puff activity in the cell interior, and the similar termination of internal and peripheral puff flurries during the rising of global Ca2+ signals, we conclude that the diffuse component of the Ca2+ rise observed by TIRF microscopy cannot be accounted for by Ca2+ spreading from punctate release at internal sites and becoming blurred by diffusion in space and time.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of lattice light-sheet data.

claim: To obtain a rate constant for removal of cytosolic Ca2+ in WT HEK cells, the decline of fluorescence Ca2+ signals following transient photorelease of Ca2+ from caged Ca2+ and during the final 'tail' of CCH-evoked Ca2+ signals were recorded.
source: To obtain a rate constant for removal of cytosolic Ca2+ in WT HEK cells, we recorded the decline of fluorescence Ca2+ signals following transient photorelease of Ca2+ from caged Ca2+ loaded into the cytosol (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), and during the final 'tail' of CCH-evoked Ca2+ signals when Ca2+ liberation would have almost ceased (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the method used to determine Ca2+ removal kinetics.

claim: Both Ca2+ removal measurements fitted well to single exponential decay functions, consistent with a dominantly first order removal process, with respective mean rate constants of 0.22 and 0.32 s−1.
source: Both fitted well to single exponential decay functions, consistent with a dominantly first order removal process, with respective mean rate constants of 0.22 and 0.32 s−1.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: From the respective areas under the Ca2+ release traces, it is estimated that, in normal conditions, the punctate liberation of Ca2+ through puff activity contributes about 41% of the total Ca2+ release responsible for the initial rise of Ca2+ toward its peak.
source: From these respective areas, we estimate that, in normal conditions, the punctate liberation of Ca2+ through puff activity contributes about 41% of the total Ca2+ release responsible for the initial rise of Ca2+ toward its peak.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Ca2+ puffs on average contribute only about 13% of the total Ca2+ liberation during global i-IP3-evoked signals, and about 17% during shorter-lasting responses evoked by CCH.
source: Because much of the cumulative Ca2+ release through IP3Rs arises from a sustained, low level flux that continues after the peak, Ca2+ puffs on average contribute only about 13% of the total Ca2+ liberation during global i-IP3-evoked signals, and about 17% during shorter-lasting responses evoked by CCH (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Ca2+ puffs are transient, localized elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ that arise from concerted opening of small numbers of IP3Rs clustered at fixed intracellular sites.
source: Ca2+ puffs are transient, localized elevations in cytosolic Ca2+ that arise from concerted opening of small numbers of IP3Rs clustered at fixed intracellular sites (Parker and Yao, 1991; Thillaiappan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Puffs are apparent as discrete events superimposed on a steady basal Ca2+ level when cytosolic IP3 concentrations are modestly elevated.
source: Puffs are apparent as discrete events superimposed on a steady basal Ca2+ level when cytosolic IP3 concentrations are modestly elevated (Parker and Yao, 1991; Yao et al., 1995; Parker et al., 1996),
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher concentrations of IP3 evoke global, cell-wide Ca2+ signals on which puffs are evident on the rising phase.
source: whereas higher concentrations of IP3 evoke global, cell-wide Ca2+ signals on which puffs are evident on the rising phase (Bootman et al., 1997a; Marchant et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Puffs have been proposed as fundamental building blocks of IP3-mediated Ca2+ signaling.
source: Puffs have been proposed as fundamental building blocks of IP3-mediated Ca2+ signaling (Bootman et al., 1997a; Parker et al., 1996; Berridge, 1997; Bootman and Berridge, 1996; Marchant, 2001; Marchant et al., 1999; Mataragka and Taylor, 2018);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Puffs act as local signals in their own right at low [IP3] and mediate global Ca2+ signals at higher [IP3] by a fire-diffuse-fire mechanism whereby Ca2+ released by a puff site diffuses to activate CICR at neighboring sites.
source: acting as local signals in their own right at low [IP3] and mediating global Ca2+ signals at higher [IP3] by a fire-diffuse-fire mechanism whereby Ca2+ released by a puff site diffuses to activate CICR at neighboring sites (Bootman et al., 1997a; Parker et al., 1996; Berridge, 1997; Dawson et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The main conclusion is that global Ca2+ signals involve two modes of Ca2+ liberation through IP3Rs: 'punctate' release as a flurry of transient, local events, and a more sustained, 'diffuse' release mode.
source: Here, we addressed this topic by analyzing temporal and spatial fluctuations in Ca2+ image data to resolve local Ca2+ transients during global signals (Swaminathan et al., 2020). Our main conclusion is that global Ca2+ signals involve two modes of Ca2+ liberation through IP3Rs: 'punctate' release as a flurry of transient, local events, and a more sustained, 'diffuse' release mode.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: Maximal, saturating signals evoked by ionomycin (~19 ΔF/F0) were much higher than mean peak IP3-evoked fluorescence signals (~7 ΔF/F0), and puff activity began to decline as fluorescence rose above ~2 ΔF/F0.
source: Notably: (i) maximal, saturating signals evoked by ionomycin (~19 ΔF/F0) were much higher than mean peak IP3-evoked fluorescence signals (~7 ΔF/F0), and puff activity began to decline as fluorescence rose above ~2 ΔF/F0;
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing ionomycin and IP3-evoked responses.

claim: Patterns of puff activity using the low affinity indicator fluo-8L (Kd1.86 µM) closely matched those obtained with Cal520 (Kd320 nM).
source: (ii) we observed patterns of puff activity using the low affinity indicator fluo-8L (Kd1.86 µM) that closely matched those obtained with Cal520 (Kd320 nM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2);
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Instances of local puff activity were resolved even at the peak of IP3-evoked global fluorescence elevations.
source: (iii) we were able to resolve instances of local puff activity even at the peak of IP3-evoked global fluorescence elevations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1);
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinetics of puff activity were closely similar in cell lines individually expressing single IP3R isoforms, despite large differences in the amplitudes of the global Ca2+ signals.
source: (iv) the kinetics of puff activity were closely similar in cell lines individually expressing single IP3R isoforms, despite large differences in the amplitudes of the global Ca2+ signals (Figure 6);
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The onset and termination of puff activity during the rise of IP3-mediated global Ca2+ signals were little altered when the initial basal Ca2+ level was elevated.
source: (v) the onset and termination of puff activity during the rise of IP3-mediated global Ca2+ signals were little altered when the initial basal Ca2+ level was elevated (Figure 4A,B) or, conversely, when the global Ca2+ rise was attenuated by buffering with cytosolic EGTA (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The suppression of punctate Ca2+ liberation throughout all phases of IP3-evoked Ca2+ responses when ER Ca2+ stores were partially depleted strongly supports the proposal that Ca2+ liberation can arise in a diffuse manner, independent of local puff events.
source: Finally, the suppression of punctate Ca2+ liberation throughout all phases of IP3-evoked Ca2+ responses when ER Ca2+ stores were partially depleted (Figure 5) strongly supports our proposal that Ca2+ liberation can arise in a diffuse manner, independent of local puff events.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Flurries of puffs were evident during the initial foot of the response and peaked early during the rising phase, but then subsided during the later portion of the rising phase, with few or no transient, local Ca2+ signals evident by the time of the peak.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Bootman et al., 1997a; Marchant et al., 1999) our fluctuation analyses reveal flurries of puffs during the initial rise of IP3-mediated global Ca2+ signals. However, although puff activity was evident during the initial foot of the response and peaked early during the rising phase, it then subsided during the later portion of the rising phase, with few or no transient, local Ca2+ signals evident by the time of the peak.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: This 'noise-free' component of the fluorescence signal cannot be attributed to slow diffusion of Ca2+ liberated as puffs to fill in spaces between release sites.
source: This 'noise-free' component of the fluorescence signal cannot be attributed to slow diffusion of Ca2+ liberated as puffs to fill in spaces between release sites.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical considerations of diffusion kinetics.

claim: Diffusion of Ca2+ would be rapid (e.g. mean time of ~300 ms to diffuse 5 μm assuming an effective diffusion coefficient of 20 μm2 s−1).
source: Diffusion would be rapid (e.g. mean time of ~300 ms to diffuse 5 μm assuming an effective diffusion coefficient of 20 μm2 s−1).
evidence: This is a calculation based on known diffusion properties.

claim: The average fluorescence signal would not be expected to increase appreciably if the total amount of Ca2+ in the imaging volume remained constant during diffusion.
source: In any case, the average fluorescence signal would not be expected to increase appreciably if the total amount of Ca2+ in the imaging volume remained constant.
evidence: This is based on theoretical considerations of fluorescence imaging.

claim: The observation of large global Ca2+ signals in the absence of detectable fluorescence fluctuations definitively points to a mode of Ca2+ liberation that is independent of puff activity.
source: Finally, as noted previously, the observation of large global Ca2+ signals in the absence of detectable fluorescence fluctuations (Figure 5) definitively points to a mode of Ca2+ liberation that is independent of puff activity.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Puffs contribute only ~41% of the initial Ca2+ flux that drives the peak of the Ca2+ response, and an even smaller proportion (~15%) of the cumulative flux during its entire time course.
source: By deriving the time course of cumulative Ca2+ liberation during global responses we estimated that puffs contribute only ~41% of the initial Ca2+ flux that drives the peak of the Ca2+ response, and an even smaller proportion (~15%) of the cumulative flux during its entire time course.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: A second component of continuous, spatially diffuse release of intracellular Ca2+ is responsible for generating and sustaining a large part of whole-cell Ca2+ signals.
source: Thus, a second component of continuous, spatially diffuse release of intracellular Ca2+ is responsible for generating and sustaining a large part of whole-cell Ca2+ signals.
evidence: This claim is based on the quantitative analysis of Ca2+ release contributions.

claim: These two components (punctate and diffuse Ca2+ release) are further discriminated by procedures that selectively promoted either puff activity or global Ca2+ elevations in the absence of localized Ca2+ transients.
source: These two components are further discriminated by procedures that selectively promoted either puff activity (Dargan and Parker, 2003; Smith et al., 2009) (by cytosolic loading of slow Ca2+ buffers), or global Ca2+ elevations in the absence of localized Ca2+ transients (by partial depletion of ER Ca2+ store content).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental manipulations described in the manuscript.

claim: The accelerated puff activity during the foot and initial upstroke of the global Ca2+ signal is likely a consequence of a rising basal cytosolic Ca2+ level, resulting both from the puffs themselves and from diffuse Ca2+ liberation.
source: Small elevations of [Ca2+] promote opening of IP3R channels (Iino, 1990; Bezprozvanny et al., 1991) and increase puff frequency (Yamasaki-Mann et al., 2013). The accelerated puff activity during the foot and initial upstroke of the global Ca2+ signal is thus likely a consequence of a rising basal cytosolic Ca2+ level, resulting both from the puffs themselves and from diffuse Ca2+ liberation.
evidence: This is an inference based on known IP3R properties and observed puff kinetics.

claim: Individual puffs terminate rapidly as IP3R channels close within tens of ms via stochastic inhibition by high local Ca2+ levels and potential allosteric interactions between clustered IP3Rs at a puff site.
source: Individual puffs terminate rapidly as IP3R channels close within tens of ms (Parker et al., 1996; Bootman et al., 1997b) via stochastic inhibition by high local Ca2+ levels (Shuai et al., 2008) and potential allosteric interactions between clustered IP3Rs at a puff site (Wiltgen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on puff termination mechanisms.

claim: During the rising phase of a global Ca2+ signal, each IP3R cluster may generate a flurry of repeated puffs - indicating that although the fast-inhibitory processes that terminates individual puffs recovers quickly, a slower process terminates the flurry.
source: However, during the rising phase of a global Ca2+ signal, each IP3R cluster may generate a flurry of repeated puffs - indicating that although the fast-inhibitory processes that terminates individual puffs recovers quickly, a slower process terminates the flurry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of puff activity.

claim: Puff flurries were not suppressed by prior Ca2+ elevations, and still terminated normally during global responses when cytosolic Ca2+ levels were attenuated by buffering with EGTA.
source: This does not appear to result from IP3Rs becoming inactivated by the rise of bulk cytosolic Ca2+, because we found puff flurries were not suppressed by prior Ca2+ elevations, and still terminated normally during global responses when cytosolic Ca2+ levels were attenuated by buffering with EGTA (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Observations that partial depletion of ER Ca2+ stores suppressed puff activity during global Ca2+ responses implicate the depletion of luminal Ca2+ as a dominant mechanism responsible for terminating the local signals.
source: Instead, our observations that partial depletion of ER Ca2+ stores suppressed puff activity during global Ca2+ responses (Figure 5) implicate the depletion of luminal Ca2+ as a dominant mechanism responsible for terminating the local signals; analogous to the central role of luminal Ca2+ depletion in terminating the Ca2+ sparks mediated by ryanodine receptors (Stern et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Although individual puffs appear not to affect luminal ER [Ca2+], it is plausible that ER depletion may occur during the rapid flurries of puffs evoked at multiple sites during the rising phase of global signals.
source: Although individual puffs appear not to affect luminal ER [Ca2+] (Lock et al., 2018), it is plausible that ER depletion may occur during the rapid flurries of puffs evoked at multiple sites during the rising phase of global signals.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed puff activity patterns.

claim: The two modes of Ca2+ liberation (punctate and diffuse) might arise from two functionally and physically distinct populations of IP3Rs, or through functional regulation of the clustered IP3Rs underlying puffs such that they switch from a pulsatile to continuous mode of release.
source: The two modes of Ca2+ liberation we describe – punctate and diffuse – might, in principle, arise from two functionally and physically distinct populations of IP3Rs, or through functional regulation of the clustered IP3Rs underlying puffs such that they switch from a pulsatile to continuous mode of release.
evidence: This presents two possible mechanisms to explain the observations.

claim: A small (~30%) fraction of the IP3Rs in a cell are stationary, grouped in small clusters that are anchored at fixed sites predominantly near the plasma membrane.
source: A small (~30%) fraction of the IP3Rs in a cell are stationary (Thillaiappan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2014), grouped in small clusters that are anchored at fixed sites predominantly near the plasma membrane (Smith et al., 2009; Lock et al., 2018; Thillaiappan et al., 2017),
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The majority of IP3Rs are distributed throughout the bulk of the cytoplasm and are motile within the ER membrane.
source: whereas the majority of IP3Rs are distributed throughout the bulk of the cytoplasm and are motile within the ER membrane (Thillaiappan et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2014; Tateishi et al., 2005; Gibson and Ehrlich, 2008; Ferreri-Jacobia et al., 2005; Fukatsu et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Puffs are proposed to originate from IP3Rs within the immotile clusters that are endowed with the ability to preferentially respond to low concentrations of IP3.
source: Puffs are proposed to originate from IP3Rs within the immotile clusters that are endowed with the ability to preferentially respond to low concentrations of IP3 (Smith et al., 2009; Thillaiappan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The widely distributed, motile IP3Rs remain apparently silent under conditions when puffs are selectively activated by low concentrations of IP3 or in the presence of slow cytosolic Ca2+ buffers to inhibit global Ca2+ elevations.
source: In contrast, the widely distributed, motile IP3Rs remain apparently silent under conditions when puffs are selectively activated by low concentrations of IP3 or in the presence of slow cytosolic Ca2+ buffers to inhibit global Ca2+ elevations (Dargan and Parker, 2003; Dargan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The motile, distributed IP3Rs would be an attractive candidate for the diffusive mode of Ca2+ liberation.
source: The motile, distributed IP3Rs would be an attractive candidate for the diffusive mode of Ca2+ liberation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of motile IP3Rs.

claim: Functional differences between putative populations of IP3Rs mediating punctate and diffuse Ca2+ release cannot be attributed to their being constituted of different isoforms of IP3R, because all three isoforms mediate Ca2+ puffs and cells exclusively expressing individual isoforms generate cell-wide Ca2+ elevations involving both punctate and diffuse modes of Ca2+ liberation.
source: Functional differences between putative populations of IP3Rs mediating punctate and diffuse Ca2+ release cannot be attributed to their being constituted of different isoforms of IP3R, because all three isoforms mediate Ca2+ puffs (Mataragka and Taylor, 2018; Lock et al., 2018), and we show here that cells exclusively expressing individual isoforms generate cell-wide Ca2+ elevations involving both punctate and diffuse modes of Ca2+ liberation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and citations to prior research.

claim: The functional properties of the IP3Rs may be affected by factors including their location in the cell, their mutual proximity to enable interactions by CICR, and by their association with modulatory and anchoring proteins.
source: Instead, the functional properties of the IP3Rs may be affected by factors including their location in the cell, their mutual proximity to enable interactions by CICR, and by their association with modulatory and anchoring proteins (Prole and Taylor, 2016; Lock et al., 2019; Konieczny et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on IP3R regulation.

claim: Stimulation of the IP3/Ca2+ signaling pathway by activation of cell-surface receptors evokes repetitive oscillations in cytosolic Ca2+ in numerous cell types.
source: Stimulation of the IP3/Ca2+ signaling pathway by activation of cell-surface receptors evokes repetitive oscillations in cytosolic Ca2+ in numerous cell types (Thomas et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Signaling information is encoded in the amplitude and frequency of Ca2+ oscillations, which may have periods ranging widely from a few seconds to minutes.
source: Signaling information is encoded in the amplitude and frequency of these Ca2+ oscillations, which may have periods ranging widely from a few seconds to minutes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ca2+ oscillations.

claim: Different frequencies of Ca2+ oscillations activate distinct targets, including the selective activation of NFkB in Jurkat T cells by low frequencies.
source: Classical studies illustrate how different frequencies of Ca2+ oscillations activate distinct targets, including the selective activation of NFkB in Jurkat T cells by low frequencies (Dolmetsch et al., 1998),
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Different frequencies of Ca2+ oscillations control gene expression in RBL mast cells in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: and the frequency-dependent control of gene expression in RBL mast cells (Li et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Signaling information is not restricted to frequency and amplitude components of bulk cytosolic Ca2+ elevations, and numerous findings implicate a component of spatial Ca2+ profiling.
source: However, signaling information is not restricted to frequency and amplitude components of bulk cytosolic Ca2+ elevations, and numerous findings implicate a component of spatial Ca2+ profiling (Smedler and Uhlén, 2014; Dupont et al., 2011; Berridge et al., 2003; Thul et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Because of the restricted diffusion of free Ca2+ ions in the cytosol, the specificity of downstream signaling by Ca2+ liberated through IP3Rs will be strongly influenced by the proximity of target proteins, as well as by their Ca2+ binding kinetics.
source: Because of the restricted diffusion of free Ca2+ ions in the cytosol (Allbritton et al., 1992; Schwaller, 2010), the specificity of downstream signaling by Ca2+ liberated through IP3Rs will be strongly influenced by the proximity of target proteins, as well as by their Ca2+ binding kinetics (Samanta and Parekh, 2017; Atakpa et al., 2018; Csordás et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of Ca2+ diffusion and signaling.

claim: Based on a close juxtaposition of stationary IP3R clusters to ER-plasma membrane junctions where STIM and Orai interact to induce store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE), it has been proposed that local depletion of ER Ca2+ content at puff sites might rapidly and selectively activate SOCE, without requiring substantial overall loss of the ER Ca2+.
source: Based on a close juxtaposition of stationary IP3R clusters to ER-plasma membrane junctions where STIM and Orai interact to induce store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE) (Thillaiappan et al., 2017; Thillaiappan et al., 2019), it has been proposed that local depletion of ER Ca2+ content at puff sites might rapidly and selectively activate SOCE, without requiring substantial overall loss of the ER Ca2+ that is necessary to sustain numerous ER functions (Thillaiappan et al., 2017; Thillaiappan et al., 2019; Taylor and Machaca, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research proposing this mechanism.

claim: Puffs were unaffected by removal of extracellular Ca2+, and patterning of local puff activity during IP3-evoked global Ca2+ signals is unaffected by the presence or absence of Ca2+ in the bath solution.
source: On the other hand, we previously reported puffs to be unaffected by removal of extracellular Ca2+ (Lock et al., 2018), and we show that patterning of local puff activity during IP3-evoked global Ca2+ signals is unaffected by the presence or absence of Ca2+ in the bath solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and citation to prior work.

claim: Influx of extracellular Ca2+ does not appear to contribute acutely to the initial flurry of puffs or to the rapid rise in global Ca2+, although the more prolonged decay phase of the Ca2+ signal in Ca2+-containing medium points to a slower activation of SOCE.
source: Thus, influx of extracellular Ca2+ does not appear to contribute acutely to the initial flurry of puffs or to the rapid rise in global Ca2+, although the more prolonged decay phase of the Ca2+ signal in Ca2+-containing medium points to a slower activation of SOCE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed kinetics in the presence and absence of extracellular Ca2+.

claim: The close tethering between ER and mitochondria underlies a rapid shuttling of Ca2+ released through IP3Rs to the mitochondrial matrix, such that Ca2+ transients within a signaling microdomain, rather than the bulk cytosolic Ca2+ signal, regulate mitochondrial bioenergetics and induction of autophagy.
source: Another example of proximate Ca2+ signaling is the close tethering between ER and mitochondria (Giorgi et al., 2009) that underlies a rapid shuttling of Ca2+ released through IP3Rs to the mitochondrial matrix (Csordás et al., 2010; Filadi and Pozzan, 2015), such that Ca2+ transients within a signaling microdomain, rather than the bulk cytosolic Ca2+ signal, regulate mitochondrial bioenergetics and induction of autophagy (Cárdenas et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A similar close coupling has recently been described between IP3Rs and lysosomes.
source: A similar close coupling has recently been described between IP3Rs and lysosomes (Atakpa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent research.
